claim: The Duomo complex sells three passes in 2026: Brunelleschi Pass EUR 30 (Dome, Bell Tower, Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata), Giotto Pass EUR 20 (no Dome), and Ghiberti Pass EUR 15 (Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata only).
quote: Brunelleschi Pass - €30 ... Dome, Bell Tower, Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata; Giotto Pass - €20 ... Bell Tower, Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata; Ghiberti Pass - €15 ... Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata

claim: Only the Brunelleschi Pass includes the cupola climb; the Dome can be entered within 3 calendar days of the chosen date but climbing it requires respecting the exact reserved date and time slot, and an ID document is required to climb from 1 March 2025.
quote: to climb-up the Dome it is mandatory to respect the chosen date and time slot ... from 1 March 2025, an identity document is required to access the climb to the Dome

claim: The dome climb requires a mandatory fixed timed slot (late arrival can forfeit it) and is 463 steps; Giotto's Bell Tower is a 414-step climb to 84 metres; the cathedral interior itself is free with no ticket required.
quote: The entry time on your ticket is fixed. Late arrival may mean losing your slot ... 463 steps from the Porta della Mandorla entrance to the lantern ... 414-step climb to the top of Giotto's Bell Tower (84 metres) ... the cathedral interior is free and always accessible outside service times

claim: Palazzo Vecchio museum admission is around EUR 13.50 for the museum alone or EUR 22 combined with the Arnolfo Tower; the museum opens Fri-Wed 9:00-19:00 and Thu 9:00-14:00, with the tower closing earlier.
quote: €13.50 for the museum alone or €22 combined with the Arnolfo Tower ... Museum opening hours are Friday to Wednesday, 9:00 AM - 7:00 PM; Thursday, 9:00 AM - 2:00 PM

claim: Palazzo Vecchio's Salone dei Cinquecento is a single hall 54 m long and 23 m wide, frescoed floor-to-ceiling by Giorgio Vasari and his workshop between 1563 and 1565 depicting Florentine military victories.
quote: a single hall 54 meters long and 23 meters wide, covered ceiling and walls with a vast fresco cycle of Florentine military victories painted by Giorgio Vasari and his workshop between 1563 and 1565

claim: Santa Croce adult admission is EUR 10 (2026), with a EUR 1 per-ticket online booking fee; children under 12, disabled visitors with companions, and Florence residents enter free.
quote: adult entrance fee is 10 Euros ... a booking fee of €1 for each ticket ... Children under 12 years old, disabled people and their companions, and residents of the City of Florence enter for free

claim: Santa Croce is the pantheon of Florence with nearly 300 tombs including those of Michelangelo Buonarroti, Galileo Galilei and Niccolo Machiavelli, and the standard ticket also covers the cloisters and museum.
quote: housing almost 300 tombs, including that of Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli ... covers access to the basilica, tombs, cloisters, and the museum section

claim: The Medici Chapels standard ticket (around EUR 9 / USD 9 in 2025, plus a EUR 3 online booking fee) covers the Medici Crypts, Michelangelo's New Sacristy and the Chapel of the Princes, accessed via a separate entrance behind San Lorenzo.
quote: standard entry ticket is $9 full price for adults in 2025 ... includes entrance to the Medici Crypts, New Sacristy, and Prince's Chapel ... accessible by a separate entrance at the back of the church of San Lorenzo

claim: Michelangelo designed and built the New Sacristy from 1519 to house the tombs of Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, decorating them with his sculptures.
quote: The New Sacristy was designed and built by Michelangelo from 1519 to house the tombs of Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, which were decorated with his wonderful sculptures

claim: The current Ponte Vecchio is a medieval closed-spandrel segmental arch bridge dating to c.1339-1345, the only Florence bridge spared in WWII; in 1593 Grand Duke Ferdinando I evicted the butchers in favour of goldsmiths and silversmiths, and the Vasari Corridor (1565) runs above it.
quote: the only bridge in Florence spared from destruction during World War II ... Ferdinando I ... issued a decree in 1593 evicting the artisans ... in favour of goldsmiths and silversmiths ... In 1565 Cosimo I de' Medici had Giorgio Vasari build the Vasari Corridor

claim: Many of the Ponte Vecchio goldsmith shops are still run by families that have worked there for generations, keeping traditional craftsmanship alive; the Vasari Corridor reopened in 2024 for guided visits.
quote: many of them are still run by families who have been working there for generations ... the Vasari Corridor reopened in 2024 for guided visits
